tool.name: Tailwind CSS
tool.tagline: Utility-first CSS framework: style by composing small classes in your markup
tool.description: Tailwind CSS provides thousands of small single-purpose classes such as flex, pt-4 and text-center that you combine directly in HTML or components. Version 4 is configured in CSS with @theme, builds on native cascade layers and CSS variables, and detects the classes you use automatically. It's one of the most popular ways to style React, Vue, Svelte and server-rendered apps quickly and consistently.

glossary.def: Running a tool that turns the files you write into the files a site actually serves, such as Tailwind turning your class names into a finished CSS file.
A free program that lets your computer run tools and programs written in JavaScript outside a browser. Most web build tools, Tailwind included, need it.
The tool that comes with Node.js for downloading and installing JavaScript tools and libraries. npx runs one of those tools directly without a separate install.
How Tailwind finds the classes to generate: it reads every text file in your project looking for class names, with no list of files to configure.
The small set of base styles Tailwind applies first. It removes the browser's default margins, heading sizes and list bullets so that every style is one you chose.
The fixed menu of spacing steps, colours, font sizes and other values that Tailwind utilities draw from, so that p-4 or text-lg means the same thing everywhere.
A reusable piece of a page, such as a button or a card, written once and used in many places. In tools like React and Vue it is the main unit you build with.
A prefix such as hover:, md: or dark: that makes a Tailwind utility apply only in that state, screen size or theme.
A slash and a number after a Tailwind colour, like bg-black/50, that makes the colour partly see-through.
Tailwind's list of named design values (colours, fonts, sizes, breakpoints), declared in an @theme block in CSS; utilities are generated from it.
A custom property declared inside @theme, such as --color-brand-500. Tailwind creates matching utilities from it (bg-brand-500) and also writes it out as a normal CSS variable.
In Tailwind, the first part of a theme variable's name, such as --color- or --font-, which decides what kind of utilities it creates.
A CSS value written in square brackets in a class name, such as w-[37px], for a one-off value that is not on the design scale.
A whole CSS declaration written as a class in square brackets, such as [mask-type:luminance], for a property Tailwind has no utility for.
A selector written in square brackets as a variant, such as [&>li]:py-2, where & stands for the element itself.
A label such as length: or color: inside a Tailwind value, as in text-(length:--size), telling Tailwind which kind of value a variable holds when it could be either.
The CSS directive for adding your own Tailwind utility class, which then works with every variant like the built-in ones.
The CSS directive for defining your own variant prefix, such as a theme-midnight: variant, or for changing how dark: is triggered.
The CSS directive that loads a Tailwind add-on written in JavaScript, such as the official typography plugin.
The CSS directive that copies Tailwind utilities into one of your own CSS rules, for example .btn { @apply px-4 py-2; }.
The CSS directive that lets a separately processed style block (a Vue or Svelte component, a CSS module) see your main stylesheet's theme without duplicating its CSS.
The CSS directive that tells Tailwind extra files or folders to scan for class names, or ones to skip.
To force specific classes into the generated CSS even though Tailwind did not find them in your files, with @source inline().
The engine inside Tailwind v4, written in Rust, that scans your files for class names and generates the CSS very fast.
A ! at the end of a Tailwind class, such as mt-0!, that adds !important to its declaration so it beats conflicting rules.
A popular tool that packs a web project's files for the browser and shows the page at a local preview address while you work. Tailwind has an official Vite plugin.
A tool that runs plugins over CSS files to transform them; one way to run Tailwind inside other build tools.
A small JavaScript library that removes conflicting Tailwind classes from a class string so that the later one wins, as when a component accepts extra classes.
A small JavaScript helper that joins class names together, including only the ones whose condition is true.
The fast CSS processor Tailwind v4 uses on its output to add browser-specific prefixes, flatten nesting and shrink the file.

concepts.name: Installing Tailwind v4
concepts.summary: Add Tailwind v4 to a project: install it, switch it on with one `@import` line, and let it build your CSS file for you.
concepts.why: Version 4 setup is much simpler than v3, and older tutorials with tailwind.config.js no longer match what you'll see.
concepts.body:
Tailwind is not a stylesheet you link and forget. It's a program that runs on your computer while you work: it reads your HTML (and other files) to see which class names you used, then writes a CSS file containing exactly those classes. Running a tool like this to produce the finished files is called a **build step**.

So you need two things installed first. **Node.js** is a free program that lets your computer run tools written in JavaScript. It comes with **npm**, which downloads and installs such tools. You use both from the **terminal**: the text window where you type commands instead of clicking icons.

In v4 there is no settings file to write. Setup is two pieces.

- **Run Tailwind.** The simplest way is Tailwind's **CLI** (command-line tool: a program you run by typing in the terminal): `npx @tailwindcss/cli -i input.css -o output.css --watch`. It reads `input.css`, writes `output.css`, and `--watch` rebuilds the output every time you save. (`npx` runs a tool from npm without a separate install.)
- **Import Tailwind.** In `input.css`, write one line: `@import "tailwindcss";`. That pulls in the default colours and sizes, a small set of base styles called Preflight (next lesson), and all the classes.

Link `output.css` in your HTML, add classes, and refresh. Tailwind finds the classes you use on its own; this is **content detection**. It looks through your project folder, skipping files it doesn't need, such as images, CSS files and anything listed in `.gitignore`. There is no list of files to maintain.

Many projects already use a **bundler**: a tool such as **Vite** that packs your files together for the browser and shows the page at a local preview address while you work. Tailwind has an official add-on for Vite, called a **plugin**: `@tailwindcss/vite`. Other setups use `@tailwindcss/postcss`, and **frameworks** (larger toolkits such as Next.js or Laravel that give a ready-made structure to build in) document their own one-step setup.

Worth installing: the Tailwind CSS IntelliSense editor add-on, which suggests class names as you type, and the Prettier plugin `prettier-plugin-tailwindcss`, which sorts your classes into a consistent order.

Tailwind v4 works only in current browsers: Safari 16.4+, Chrome 111+ and Firefox 128+. If you must support older ones, stay on v3.4.
concepts.code:
# In the terminal, inside your project folder (needs Node.js): npm install tailwindcss @tailwindcss/cli npx @tailwindcss/cli -i src/input.css -o src/output.css --watch # -i = the file to read, -o = the file to write, --watch = keep rebuilding # src/input.css is one line: # @import "tailwindcss"; # index.html links the GENERATED file and just uses classes: # #

Hello Tailwind

# With Vite instead of the CLI: npm install tailwindcss @tailwindcss/vite, # then add tailwindcss() to the plugins list in vite.config.js.
takeaways: Tailwind is a build step: it writes a CSS file with only the classes you use
Setup = run Tailwind (CLI, Vite plugin or PostCSS) + @import "tailwindcss"
Class detection is automatic, with no list of files to maintain
v4 needs Safari 16.4+, Chrome 111+, Firefox 128+
pitfalls: Following a v3 tutorial that uses @tailwind base/components/utilities and a tailwind.config.js file; v4 needs neither.

quiz.q: What replaces the three @tailwind lines of v3 in a v4 stylesheet?
options: Nothing; v4 needs no CSS file
quiz.explain: A single @import brings in the theme, the base styles and all the utilities.

quiz.q: Tailwind offers thousands of classes, yet the generated output.css is small. Why?
options: It only writes the classes it found in your project's files
It compresses every class into one line
The browser downloads the rest when needed
You must list the classes you want in a settings file
quiz.explain: Content detection scans your files and generates CSS only for the class names it actually sees.

concepts.name: The utility-first workflow
concepts.summary: Style elements by combining small single-purpose classes in the markup instead of writing custom CSS rules.
concepts.why: Understanding the trade-offs explains why Tailwind code looks the way it does and when it pays off.
concepts.body:
In traditional CSS you invent a class name, `.profile-card`, and write its rules in a stylesheet. Tailwind turns that around. It gives you thousands of ready-made **utility classes**, each doing exactly one job: `p-6` adds padding, `rounded-xl` rounds the corners, `shadow-lg` adds a shadow. You combine them right in the HTML:

```html
<div class="mx-auto max-w-sm rounded-xl bg-white p-6 shadow-lg">
```

Every utility stands for one or a few CSS declarations. Its values come from a shared **design scale**: a fixed menu of spacing steps, colours and font sizes. `p-6` is always the same amount of padding, wherever you use it.

Why people like it:

- No naming: you never invent class names or switch between the HTML and a CSS file.
- Styles are local: changing a class changes only that element, so there's no fear of breaking a distant page.
- CSS stops growing: the same utilities are reused everywhere, and classes you never use are never written to the file.
- Consistency: every value comes from the design scale, so pages look like they belong together.

Two common objections have answers. First, class lists get long. The fix is not custom CSS; it's reuse. Put the piece of HTML in one place and use it many times. In tools such as React or Vue that reusable piece is called a **component**; in a server-made site it's a template partial, a snippet of HTML included on many pages.

Second, isn't this just inline styles? No. Utilities can respond to hover, keyboard focus, screen size and dark mode (the next lessons show how), which a `style` attribute never can.

One surprise on day one: **Preflight**, the base styles Tailwind applies before anything else, resets the browser's defaults. Headings and paragraphs lose their built-in margins and sizes, and lists lose their bullets. That's deliberate, so every visual choice is one you made with a utility. Add classes to style them, or use the typography plugin (an add-on that styles whole articles at once) for long text.
concepts.code:
Ada Lovelace

Wrote the first program
takeaways: Each utility does one thing, with values from a shared design scale
Reuse through components or partials, not custom class names
Preflight removes the browser's default styles on purpose
pitfalls: Wondering why h1 and ul look unstyled: Preflight resets them; add utilities.

quiz.q: In a Tailwind project, an h1 renders at normal text size. Why?
options: Preflight resets heading styles; you add text-* utilities
quiz.explain: Preflight removes the default heading sizes and margins so that all styling is explicit.

concepts.name: Spacing and sizing
concepts.summary: Use the spacing scale for padding, margin, gap, width and height, including fractions, size-* and any whole number like p-13.
concepts.why: Spacing and sizing utilities are the classes you'll type most.
concepts.body:
Every spacing utility in Tailwind v4 is built from one base step, `--spacing`, which is `0.25rem` (4px) unless you change it. The number in a class is a multiple of that step: `p-4` means `calc(var(--spacing) * 4)`, which is 1rem. Any whole number works, so `p-13` or `mt-17` are valid without any setup. (`--spacing` is a **custom property**: a CSS value you name yourself and read back with `var()`. The CSS lessons cover them properly later.)

**Padding and margin**: `p-4` (all sides), `px-4`/`py-2` (left and right / top and bottom), `pt-2`, `pr-3`, `pb-4`, `pl-5`, and the logical `ps-4`/`pe-4` (start/end, which flip for right-to-left languages). Margins mirror them with `m-`, plus `mx-auto` for centring and negative margins like `-mt-2`.

**Gaps**: `gap-4`, `gap-x-2`, `gap-y-6` put space between the items of a flex or grid container. Prefer gap over margins between siblings. (`space-y-4` adds margins between children when you're not in flex or grid.)

**Width and height**:

- scale values: `w-64`, `h-10`,
- fractions: `w-1/2`, `w-2/3`,
- named sizes: `w-full` (100%), `w-screen` (100vw), `h-dvh`, `w-fit`, `w-min`, `w-max`,
- both at once: `size-10` sets width and height.

**Limits**: `max-w-prose` (65ch, a comfortable line length), `max-w-md` and friends (`max-w-md` is 28rem), `min-h-dvh`, `min-w-0`.

`p-px` gives 1px and `p-0.5` half a step. For a value that isn't on the scale, there is a square-bracket form, `w-[37px]` (covered in a later lesson), but reach for the scale first; it's what keeps a design consistent.

Sidebar
Content

Readable line length.
takeaways: Numbers are multiples of --spacing (0.25rem): p-4 = 1rem
Any whole number works without config: p-13
size-* sets width and height together
Prefer gap over margins between siblings
pitfalls: Using space-y-* on a flex or grid container, where gap-* is simpler and more robust.

concepts.name: Colours and typography
concepts.summary: Apply the colour palette with text-, bg- and border- utilities and the /50 opacity modifier, and set type with size, weight and leading utilities.
concepts.why: Colour and type utilities make up most of a component's visual style.
concepts.body:
**Colours** come from a default palette of more than twenty hues (red, orange, amber, yellow, green, emerald, teal, sky, blue, indigo, violet, purple, pink, rose and others, plus several grays such as slate, gray, zinc and stone). Each hue has shades from `50` (lightest) to `950` (darkest), written in `oklch` so that steps look evenly spaced. Use them with any colour utility:

- `text-gray-700`, `bg-indigo-600`, `border-red-500`, `decoration-sky-400` (underline colour), `ring-blue-500` (a ring is an outline-like line drawn with a shadow),
- plus `black`, `white`, `transparent` and `current` (the element's own text colour, `currentColor`).

The **opacity modifier** makes a colour partly see-through with a slash: `bg-black/50` is black at 50%, `text-white/80`, `border-gray-900/10`. It works on every colour utility and replaces v3's separate `bg-opacity-*` classes.

**Typography**:

- size: `text-xs`, `text-sm`, `text-base` (1rem), `text-lg` up to `text-9xl`. Each size comes with a matching default line height.
- line height in the same class: `text-lg/7` (size lg, line height of 7 spacing steps), or separately `leading-tight`, `leading-6`.
- weight: `font-normal`, `font-medium`, `font-semibold`, `font-bold`.
- family: `font-sans`, `font-serif`, `font-mono`.
- `tracking-tight` (letter spacing), `uppercase`, `italic`, `underline`, `truncate` (one line, cut off with ...), `line-clamp-3` (at most three lines), `text-balance` for evenly wrapped headings, `text-center`.

Choose shades with contrast in mind: `text-gray-500` on white is fine for secondary text, but lighter grays are usually too faint for body text to pass the accessibility rules for readable contrast.

Faster builds in version 4

The new engine is up to 5x faster for full builds.

Read the changelog
Tip: bg-black/50 means black at 50% opacity.
takeaways: Shades run 50 (light) to 950 (dark) on every hue
A slash makes any colour partly transparent: bg-black/50
text-lg/7 sets font size and line height together
Check that text colours contrast enough with the background
pitfalls: Using v3's bg-opacity-50 class, which v4 removed; use bg-black/50.

quiz.q: Which class gives a red-500 border at 25% opacity?
quiz.explain: The slash modifier makes that one colour partly transparent; opacity-25 would fade the whole element.

concepts.name: Flexbox and grid layouts
concepts.summary: Build layouts with flex, items-center, justify-between, grid-cols-* and col-span-* utilities.
concepts.why: Layout utilities let you build navigation bars, card grids and whole page skeletons without leaving the markup.
concepts.body:
Tailwind's layout utilities map directly onto CSS flexbox and grid. You know flexbox already; **CSS grid** is the other layout tool. It divides a container into columns and rows at once, and you place items into the cells, so things line up in both directions. This lesson shows enough grid to use it; the CSS Grid lesson goes deeper.

**Flexbox**:

- `flex` (or `inline-flex`), `flex-col` for a column, `flex-wrap`.
- Alignment: `items-center`, `items-start`, `justify-between`, `justify-center`, `self-end`.
- Item sizing: `flex-1` (grow and shrink, starting from zero width), `flex-auto`, `flex-none`, `grow`, `shrink-0`, `basis-64`.
- `gap-4` between items, `order-first` to reorder.

**Grid**:

- `grid` with `grid-cols-3` creates three equal columns. The generated CSS is `repeat(3, minmax(0, 1fr))`. The **fr unit** is one equal share of the leftover space, and `minmax(0, 1fr)` lets a column shrink below its content's width instead of pushing the layout wider than the page.
- `col-span-2` makes an item span two columns; `col-span-full` spans all of them; `col-start-2` places it in a specific column.
- `grid-rows-*`, `row-span-*`, `grid-flow-col` (fill columns instead of rows), `auto-rows-fr` (equal-height rows).
- `place-items-center` centres the content of every cell.

Centring anything takes three classes, `flex items-center justify-center`, or two: `grid place-items-center`.

A common page skeleton: `grid min-h-dvh grid-rows-[auto_1fr_auto]` gives a header, a content area that fills the rest and a footer. A sidebar layout: `flex` on the wrapper, `w-64 shrink-0` on the sidebar and `min-w-0 flex-1` on the content, where `min-w-0` lets long content shrink instead of overflowing.

Layout classes combine with the screen-size prefixes covered in the responsive lesson: `grid-cols-1 md:grid-cols-3` is one column on phones and three on wider screens.

concepts.name: Hover, focus and other states
concepts.summary: Apply utilities only in certain states with variants such as hover:, focus-visible:, disabled:, group-hover:, peer-checked: and has-*.
concepts.why: Variants are how utility classes handle hover, focus and other states, which inline styles never could.
concepts.body:
A **variant** is a prefix that applies a utility only under a condition: `hover:bg-indigo-700` sets the background only while the mouse is over the element. Variants exist for nearly every pseudo-class:

- interaction: `hover:`, `focus:`, `focus-visible:`, `active:`, `focus-within:`,
- forms: `disabled:`, `checked:`, `required:`, `invalid:`, `user-invalid:`, `placeholder:` (the pseudo-element), `file:`,
- position among siblings: `first:`, `last:`, `odd:`, `even:`, `nth-3:`, `not-first:`, `empty:`,
- `open:` for details and dialogs, `before:`/`after:` for pseudo-elements, and attribute checks such as `aria-expanded:` and `data-[state=open]:`.

In v4, `hover:` is wrapped in a media query (a CSS condition) that checks the device can really hover, so tapping on a touch screen doesn't leave hover styles stuck on.

**Styling based on other elements**:

- Mark a parent with the `group` class, then use `group-hover:` or `group-focus:` on any descendant.
- Mark a sibling with `peer` and use `peer-checked:` or `peer-invalid:` on later siblings. The peer must come *before* them in the HTML, because it uses the CSS `~` combinator, which only looks forward.
- `has-checked:` and `has-[img]:` use the `:has()` selector, which picks an element by what is inside it, to style a parent by its contents.
- When groups are nested, name them to tell them apart: `group/item` on the parent and `group-hover/item:` on the child.

Variants stack: `dark:md:hover:bg-gray-700`. In v4 they apply left to right, matching the nested CSS they produce.

Read the docs →

  • Two
takeaways: Prefix any utility with a state: hover:, focus-visible:, disabled:
group / group-*: style children from a parent's state
peer / peer-*: style later siblings; the peer must come first
hover: only applies on devices that can hover
pitfalls: Putting the peer element after the element that uses peer-*; the sibling combinator only looks forward.

quiz.q: A hidden checkbox should restyle the label text that follows it. Which classes?
options: group on the text, group-checked: on the checkbox
peer on the checkbox, peer-checked: on the text
quiz.explain: peer marks the earlier sibling; peer-checked: applies when it is checked.

concepts.name: Responsive design
concepts.summary: Build mobile-first layouts with sm:, md:, lg:, xl: and 2xl: breakpoint prefixes, plus max-* and range variants.
concepts.why: Responsive prefixes let one set of classes describe the layout for every screen size.
concepts.body:
Breakpoint variants apply a utility from a minimum width upwards:

- `sm:` 40rem (640px)
- `md:` 48rem (768px)
- `lg:` 64rem (1024px)
- `xl:` 80rem (1280px)
- `2xl:` 96rem (1536px)

Tailwind is **mobile-first**: a class with no prefix applies at every size, and a prefixed one replaces it from that width up. So `text-center sm:text-left` is centred on phones and left-aligned from 640px. A common mistake is reaching for `sm:` to target phones; the unprefixed class already does that.

To target a range, stack a `max-*` variant: `md:max-lg:flex` applies only between md and lg. `max-md:hidden` hides the element below 768px.

Breakpoints come from Tailwind's **theme**: the list of named values (colours, sizes, breakpoints) that its utilities are generated from. You can add or change one in CSS:

```css
@theme { --breakpoint-3xl: 120rem; }
```

which immediately enables `3xl:` utilities. For a one-off width there is the square-bracket form, such as `min-[320px]:text-sm`.

The media queries Tailwind generates use the newer range form, `@media (width >= 48rem)`, in rem, so they respect the reader's font-size settings.

Good responsive Tailwind usually needs fewer breakpoints than you'd think: `flex-wrap`, `grid-cols-[repeat(auto-fit,minmax(16rem,1fr))]` and percentage widths adapt continuously. Use breakpoints for structural changes, like showing the full navigation from `md:` up.

concepts.name: Dark mode
concepts.summary: Style dark themes with the dark: variant, driven by the device's dark-mode setting or by a class or data attribute you switch yourself.
concepts.why: Users expect dark mode, and Tailwind makes supporting it a matter of adding dark: classes.
concepts.body:
The `dark:` variant applies a utility when dark mode is active: `bg-white dark:bg-gray-900`.

By default it follows the dark-mode setting of the user's device, the same one that makes their other apps dark. The generated CSS is `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)`, and no JavaScript is needed.

To let users choose a theme themselves, redefine the variant in your CSS so it depends on a class or attribute instead:

```css
@custom-variant dark (&:where(.dark, .dark *));
```

Now `dark:` applies inside any element with the `dark` class, usually `<html class="dark">`. A few lines of JavaScript in the head set that class before the page is first drawn, reading a saved choice from `localStorage` (the browser's small store of saved values) or the device setting from `matchMedia`, so the user never sees a flash of the wrong theme. A data attribute works the same way: `&:where([data-theme=dark], [data-theme=dark] *)`.

Practical advice:

- Design the pairs together: `text-gray-900 dark:text-gray-100`, `border-gray-200 dark:border-white/10`. See-through whites and blacks (`bg-white/5`) adapt well to layered dark surfaces.
- Set `color-scheme` (the `scheme-light-dark` utility or plain CSS) so form controls and scrollbars match the theme.
- In larger apps, define named colours such as `--color-surface` in `@theme` (see the theme lesson), switch their values in dark mode, and use `bg-surface` and `text-muted` everywhere instead of writing `dark:` pairs on every element.
concepts.code: Card text
takeaways: dark: follows the device's prefers-color-scheme setting by default
@custom-variant dark (...) switches it to a class or attribute
Set the class in a head script to avoid a flash of the wrong theme
Named theme colours beat dark: pairs in large apps
pitfalls: Switching the dark class on only after the page has been drawn, causing a white flash on load.

quiz.q: Without any configuration, when does dark:bg-black apply in Tailwind v4?
options: Never, dark mode must be enabled in a config file
When the device or browser is set to prefer a dark colour scheme
quiz.explain: The default dark variant uses the prefers-color-scheme media query, which reflects the device setting.

concepts.name: Customising the theme with @theme
concepts.summary: Define colours, fonts, breakpoints and other design tokens in CSS with @theme, creating utilities and CSS variables at the same time.
concepts.why: @theme is how every v4 project brings in its own brand, and it replaces most of tailwind.config.js.
concepts.body:
In v4 your **theme**, the design choices (colours, fonts, sizes) that utilities are generated from, lives in CSS. **Theme variables** are custom properties declared inside an `@theme` block. The first part of a variable's name is its **namespace**, and that decides which utilities it creates:

- `--color-brand-500` creates `bg-brand-500`, `text-brand-500`, `border-brand-500` and so on,
- `--font-display` creates `font-display`,
- `--text-*`, `--font-weight-*`, `--leading-*`, `--tracking-*` for type,
- `--breakpoint-*` for responsive variants, `--container-*` for container sizes and `max-w-*`,
- `--radius-*`, `--shadow-*`, `--ease-*`, `--animate-*`, and `--spacing` for the whole spacing scale.

Every theme variable is also written out as a normal CSS variable on `:root` (when it's used), so you can read it anywhere: `var(--color-brand-500)` in custom CSS, inline styles or JavaScript.

To **extend** the theme, just add variables. To **replace** a default, declare it again with the same name. To **remove** a whole namespace, set it to `initial` (`--color-*: initial;`) and define only your own colours; `--*: initial` clears the entire default theme.

Use plain `:root` variables for values that shouldn't create utilities. Use `@theme inline` when a theme variable points at another variable, so utilities get the final value rather than a `var()` link that might resolve differently deeper in the tree.

To share a theme across projects, put the `@theme` block in its own CSS file and `@import` it.
takeaways: @theme variables generate utilities based on their namespace
They're also real CSS variables usable anywhere
Declare a name again to replace it; --color-*: initial removes a namespace
Use :root for variables that shouldn't create utilities
pitfalls: Putting brand colours in :root and wondering why bg-brand-500 doesn't exist.

quiz.q: Which declaration in @theme makes a class like shadow-glow available?

concepts.name: Container queries
concepts.summary: Make components adapt to their parent's width, not the screen's, with the @container class and @sm:, @md:, @lg: variants.
concepts.why: Components that respond to their own space can be reused anywhere without page-level breakpoints.
concepts.body:
A screen breakpoint asks how wide the whole window is. A **container query** instead asks how wide a chosen parent element is, so the same card can lay itself out differently in a narrow sidebar and a wide main column. Container queries are built into Tailwind v4. Two steps:

- Add the `@container` class to a parent, which sets `container-type: inline-size` ("measure my width").
- Use `@`-prefixed variants on descendants: `@md:flex-row` applies when the nearest container is at least `28rem` wide.

The container sizes are separate from screen breakpoints and smaller: `@3xs` (16rem), `@2xs` (18rem), `@xs` (20rem), `@sm` (24rem), `@md` (28rem), `@lg` (32rem), `@xl` (36rem), `@2xl` (42rem) and up to `@7xl` (80rem). They come from the `--container-*` theme variables, which also drive `max-w-md` and friends.

Like screen breakpoints, they're mobile-first, with `@max-md:` for the opposite direction and ranges such as `@sm:@max-md:`.

**Named containers** handle nesting: `@container/sidebar` on the parent and `@lg/sidebar:grid-cols-2` on a child target that container specifically rather than the nearest one.

One-off sizes work too: `@min-[400px]:flex`.

The `cqw` unit (1% of the container's width) and its relatives are available through square-bracket values, such as `text-[5cqw]`, for type that scales with the container.

Rule of thumb: screen breakpoints (`md:`) for the page skeleton, container variants (`@md:`) inside reusable components like cards, list items and widgets.

Designing Data-Intensive Applications

A deep dive into storage and streams.

    ...
takeaways: @container on the parent, @md: etc. on descendants
Container sizes are smaller than screen breakpoints (@md = 28rem)
Name containers with @container/name for nesting
Breakpoints for pages, container variants for components
pitfalls: Using @md: without any @container parent above it, so the variant never applies.

quiz.q: Why does @md:flex-row not apply to a card with no @container class above it?
options: Container variants measure the nearest parent marked as a container, and there is none
flex-row isn't allowed with container variants
quiz.explain: Without an ancestor marked as a container there is nothing for the query to measure.

concepts.name: Arbitrary values and properties
concepts.summary: Escape the design scale with square-bracket values like w-[37px], the CSS-variable shorthand bg-(--x), and arbitrary properties.
concepts.why: Real designs always have a few one-off values, and this is how you handle them without leaving the markup.
concepts.body:
When the scale doesn't have what you need, put any CSS value in square brackets. This is an **arbitrary value**:

- `w-[37px]`, `top-[117px]`, `bg-[#bada55]`, `grid-cols-[200px_1fr_auto]`.
- Spaces are written as underscores, because class names can't contain spaces: `grid-rows-[auto_1fr_auto]`. Write `\_` for a real underscore.
- CSS functions work: `w-[calc(100%-2rem)]`, `h-[min(50vh,30rem)]`.

**CSS variables** have a shorthand with parentheses: `bg-(--brand-color)` becomes `background-color: var(--brand-color)`. (In v3 this was written `bg-[--brand-color]`.) That's the clean way to pass changing values from JavaScript: set `style="--progress: 40%"` on the element and use `w-(--progress)`.

When a value could mean two things, add a **type hint**: `text-(length:--size)` is a font size, while `text-(color:--accent)` is a colour.

**Arbitrary properties** turn any CSS declaration into a class, with variants still available: `[mask-type:luminance]`, `hover:[mask-type:alpha]`.

**Arbitrary variants** build a selector on the fly, with `&` standing for the element itself: `[&>*]:p-4` styles all direct children, `[&:nth-child(3)]:underline`, and `data-[state=open]:rotate-180`.

Use these sparingly. If the same arbitrary value appears in several places, it belongs in `@theme` as a named value. And class names must appear complete in your files; you can't build `w-[${n}px]` from pieces while the page runs, because Tailwind never sees it (more on this in Class detection).

...
  • One
  • Two
takeaways: Square brackets take any value; underscores stand for spaces
bg-(--var) is shorthand for var(--var)
Arbitrary properties [prop:value] and variants [&>li]: work with modifiers
Repeated one-offs belong in @theme
pitfalls: Building class names from pieces, like `w-[${n}px]`, which Tailwind's file scan can't see.

quiz.q: How do you write grid-template-columns: 1fr 300px as a Tailwind class?
quiz.explain: Spaces aren't allowed in class names, so underscores stand in for them.

concepts.name: Custom utilities and variants
concepts.summary: Register your own utilities with @utility (including functional ones with --value()) and your own variants with @custom-variant.
concepts.why: When the same styling repeats across a codebase, a first-class utility or variant keeps markup clean and consistent.
takeaways: @utility adds utilities that work with all variants
Functional utilities use name-* and --value()
@custom-variant defines new variants; @variant uses one inside CSS
@plugin loads JS plugins such as typography
pitfalls: Writing custom utilities as plain classes inside @layer utilities, where v4 no longer treats them as variant-aware utilities; use @utility.

quiz.q: You define @utility tab-* { tab-size: --value(integer); }. Which class works?

concepts.name: Reuse: components, @apply and class merging
concepts.summary: Avoid duplication by extracting components, use @apply sparingly, and manage conflicting classes with helpers like clsx and tailwind-merge.
concepts.why: Long repeated class lists are the main maintenance cost of Tailwind, and these habits keep it under control.
concepts.body:
The answer to "my class lists repeat" is usually **a component**, not CSS. Put the markup in a React, Vue or Svelte component, a template partial, or even a loop, and the classes exist in one place.

**Versions of a component** (primary/secondary, sm/lg) are best expressed as a lookup from the component's inputs (its props) to class strings. Libraries such as `cva` (class-variance-authority) formalise this. Two helpers are widely used:

- `clsx` joins classes conditionally: `clsx("px-4", active && "bg-indigo-600")`.
- `tailwind-merge` resolves conflicts so the later class wins: `twMerge("px-4 py-2", "px-6")` gives `"py-2 px-6"`. Without it, both `px-4` and `px-6` would be present and the winner would depend on their order in the generated stylesheet, not on their order in the class attribute.

**@apply** copies utilities into your own CSS rule: `.btn { @apply rounded-md px-4 py-2; }`. It's reasonable for HTML you don't control (CMS output, third-party widgets) or very small shared pieces. Overusing it recreates traditional CSS, with naming and growing stylesheets, and gives up the benefits.

In v4, the style blocks inside components (Vue `<style>`, Svelte, CSS modules) are processed separately from your main stylesheet, so `@apply` and theme variables there need `@reference "../app.css";` at the top. It loads the theme for lookup without duplicating any CSS in the output.

Keep class order consistent with the Prettier plugin; it makes long lists far easier to scan.
takeaways: Extract components first; @apply second
Model component variants as a lookup from props to classes
tailwind-merge makes the later of two conflicting classes win
Vue/Svelte style blocks need @reference to use @apply
pitfalls: Passing className="px-6" to a component that already has px-4 without merging; which one wins depends on stylesheet order.

quiz.q: Without tailwind-merge, an element has class="px-6 px-4". Which padding applies?
options: Whichever rule comes later in the generated stylesheet
px-6, because it comes first in the attribute
px-4, because it comes last in the attribute
quiz.explain: Class attribute order is irrelevant in CSS; stylesheet order and specificity decide.

concepts.name: Class detection and the build engine
concepts.summary: Know how v4's Rust-powered engine finds class names in your files, why class names built from pieces fail, and how @source and safelisting work.
concepts.why: Missing styles in production almost always come from class names the scanner couldn't see.
concepts.body:
Tailwind doesn't run your code. Its engine (Oxide, written in Rust) reads your files as plain text, pulls out every word-like chunk that could be a class name, and generates CSS for the ones that match a utility. Chunks that match nothing are ignored, so scanning is fast and over-inclusive rather than precise.

Consequences:

- Class names must appear **complete** in the source. `text-${color}-600` is never seen; map values to full strings instead: `{ red: "text-red-600", green: "text-green-600" }[color]`.
- Classes in comments or strings still generate CSS (harmless).
- Classes that only arrive while the app runs, such as from a database or a CMS, need to be listed somewhere the scanner looks.

**What gets scanned**: everything in the project except files listed in `.gitignore`, non-text files, CSS files and lock files. The base path is the current working directory. Tools for special cases:

- `@source "../node_modules/@acme/ui";` adds a path, such as a component library inside `node_modules` (skipped by default).
- `@source not "./legacy";` excludes a path.
- `@import "tailwindcss" source("../src");` sets the base path; `source(none)` turns off automatic detection so only explicit `@source` paths are used, which suits a monorepo (one repository holding several projects).
- `@source inline("underline bg-red-{100..900..100}");` **safelists** classes, forcing them into the output; the braces expand to a range.

The build runs incrementally: only changed files are rescanned and new utilities appended, which is why rebuilds take milliseconds. The output is then passed through Lightning CSS, which adds browser-specific prefixes, flattens nesting and minifies the file.
takeaways: The scanner reads files as text: class names must appear complete
node_modules and .gitignore'd paths are skipped by default
@source adds or excludes paths; source() sets the base
@source inline() safelists classes
pitfalls: Building class names from pieces and seeing the styles only in development, where they happened to exist in another file.

quiz.q: A component renders className={`text-${tone}-600`}. Why are the colours missing?
options: Template literals are not allowed in JSX
The scanner only sees complete class names in source text
quiz.explain: Tailwind never executes code, so text-red-600 never appears in the source and isn't generated.

concepts.name: Layers, Preflight and specificity
concepts.summary: See how v4 organises its output into native cascade layers, why utilities beat component classes, and how the important modifier works.
concepts.why: Understanding the generated CSS explains every 'why doesn't my class win?' question in Tailwind projects.
concepts.body:
Tailwind v4 writes its CSS into native **cascade layers** in this order: `@layer theme, base, components, utilities;`.

- **theme**: the `:root` CSS variables for the theme values in use.
- **base**: Preflight, a reset built on modern-normalize (a small stylesheet that evens out browser differences): margins removed, `box-sizing: border-box`, borders set to `0 solid`, images block-level, headings unstyled.
- **components**: empty by default; your own component classes go here via `@layer components { ... }`.
- **utilities**: every generated utility and every `@utility` you define.

Because layer order beats specificity, any utility overrides any component class, however specific its selector. That's why `class="btn px-8"` reliably gets `px-8`.

**Unlayered CSS beats all layers.** Custom CSS written after the `@import` without a `@layer` wrapper overrides utilities, which surprises people moving from v3. Wrap such styles in a layer, typically `components`.

Utilities are mostly single-class selectors with equal specificity, so among utilities the generated order decides. Tailwind sorts them deliberately: shorthand before longhand (`px-4` comes after `p-2` so it wins), and variants after base utilities, with breakpoints ordered small to large.

The **important modifier** is a `!` at the end: `bg-red-500!` adds `!important`. And `@import "tailwindcss" important;` marks all utilities important, for dropping Tailwind into pages whose existing CSS is aggressive.

v4 also registers some internal custom properties with `@property`, giving each a type and an initial value, which is what lets gradient stops and shadow colours combine and animate correctly.
takeaways: Layer order: theme, base, components, utilities
Utilities beat component classes regardless of specificity
Unlayered custom CSS beats all utilities: wrap it in a layer
The ! suffix (bg-red-500!) adds !important
pitfalls: Writing unlayered custom CSS in v4 and finding utility classes no longer override it.

quiz.q:
Custom CSS '.card p { margin: 0 }' is written after @import "tailwindcss" without @layer. What happens to

inside .card?
options: mt-4 wins because utilities always win
The unlayered rule wins, so margin-top is 0
The build fails with a conflict error
quiz.explain: Unlayered styles beat every cascade layer, including utilities.

concepts.name: Upgrading from v3 and browser support
concepts.summary: Migrate v3 projects with the official upgrade tool and know the renamed utilities, changed defaults and modern-browser requirements of v4.
concepts.why: Many codebases and tutorials are still v3; knowing the differences prevents subtle visual regressions.
concepts.body:
v4 is a rewrite with CSS-first configuration. The official tool does most of a migration: `npx @tailwindcss/upgrade` (run it on a clean branch) updates dependencies, converts `tailwind.config.js` into `@theme` and CSS directives, and rewrites class names in templates.

What changes and why it matters:

- **Imports**: `@tailwind base; @tailwind components; @tailwind utilities;` becomes `@import "tailwindcss";`. The CLI and PostCSS plugin moved to `@tailwindcss/cli` and `@tailwindcss/postcss`.
- **Renamed scales**: the old unnamed `shadow`, `rounded` and `blur` are now `shadow-sm`, `rounded-sm` and `blur-sm`, and the old `-sm` versions became `-xs`. `outline-none` is `outline-hidden`; `flex-shrink-0` is `shrink-0`.
- **Removed**: `bg-opacity-*` and similar opacity utilities; use the `/50` modifier.
- **Changed defaults**: borders and dividers default to `currentColor` instead of gray-200; `ring` is 1px instead of 3px; placeholder text uses the current colour at 50%; buttons use `cursor: default`.
- **Class spelling**: variants stack left to right, the important modifier moves to the end (`bg-red-500!`), and CSS-variable values use `bg-(--x)`. Use `var(--color-red-500)` in CSS instead of `theme()`.

**Browser support** is the one hard limit. v4 relies on `@property`, cascade layers and `color-mix()`, so it needs Safari 16.4+, Chrome 111+ and Firefox 128+. Projects that must support older browsers should stay on v3.4.
concepts.code:
# Migrate a v3 project (on a clean git branch)
npx @tailwindcss/upgrade

# Typical class changes the tool rewrites:
#   shadow-sm        -> shadow-xs
#   shadow           -> shadow-sm
#   rounded          -> rounded-sm
#   outline-none     -> outline-hidden
#   flex-shrink-0    -> shrink-0
#   bg-opacity-50    -> bg-black/50  (merged into the colour)
#   !mt-0            -> mt-0!
#   bg-[--brand]     -> bg-(--brand)

# Default changes to review visually afterwards:
#   border  -> currentColor instead of gray-200 (add border-gray-200 where needed)
#   ring    -> 1px instead of 3px (use ring-3 for the old look)
git diff --stat
takeaways: Run npx @tailwindcss/upgrade on a clean branch
Unnamed scale steps shifted: shadow -> shadow-sm, shadow-sm -> shadow-xs
Borders default to currentColor and ring to 1px
v4 requires Safari 16.4+, Chrome 111+, Firefox 128+
pitfalls: Trusting the automated upgrade without visually checking borders and rings, whose defaults changed.

quiz.q: After upgrading, bare 'border' elements suddenly look dark. Why?
options: Dark mode is on by default
The default border colour is now currentColor instead of gray-200
quiz.explain: v4 aligned the border default with CSS, which uses currentColor.
